analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to accurately classify and give written notice to workers, with penalties for misclassification.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in House committees when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many companies label workers as independent contractors instead of employees, which strips those workers of minimum wage, overtime, and unemployment coverage and lets the companies avoid payroll taxes. This bill would have required every employer to keep records showing each worker's classification, hand every worker a written notice stating their classification and their rights, and double the damages owed when an employer misclassifies workers to dodge wage laws. It would also have pressured states to audit employers who underreport wages and to fine companies that misclassify workers for unemployment tax purposes.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are misclassified as independent contractors gain clearer information about their status, easier ways to challenge it, and doubled back wages when employers cheat on minimum wage or overtime. Honest employers who already classify correctly would face less unfair competition from companies that cut costs by misclassifying.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must keep records of every contractor and give each worker written notice of whether they are classified as an employee or not, including a statement telling them how to contact the Labor Department if they suspect misclassification [S2] [S3].

Deliberately misclassifying a worker becomes a distinct violation of the Fair Labor Standards Act, and liquidated damages for minimum wage and overtime violations are doubled when the employer also violated the classification rules [S2] [S3].
Repeat or willful violators of the notice rules face civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation [S2] [S3].

States must run audit programs to find employers excluding workers from unemployment coverage and set administrative penalties for misclassification, as a condition of federal unemployment administration grants [S2] [S3].

The Labor Department must route misclassification information it discovers to its enforcement arm and may share it with the IRS, and must direct at least a quarter of wage-and-hour audits at record-keeping and classification violations in high-misclassification industries [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on independent-contractor arrangements bear the cost of record-keeping and written notices, and those that misclassify workers face doubled damages and fines. They also lose the payroll tax and wage savings that misclassification provides. State unemployment agencies take on new auditing duties.

drawbacks.text: Every employer in the country, including those that classify correctly, would face new record-keeping and written-notice paperwork for contractors, an administrative cost borne by businesses of all sizes [S2] [S3].

The bill does not rewrite the legal test for who counts as an employee, so workers would get clearer notices about a classification they may still be unable to successfully challenge, and employers would face penalties under a standard that remains genuinely uncertain.
Routing Labor Department misclassification findings to the IRS increases the chance that workers classified as contractors, as well as employers, get drawn into tax enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is transparency: workers would at least know how they were classified and where to complain, and employers who cheat on wages would owe more. The honest cost is paperwork for every employer, and the honest limitation is that the bill sharpens enforcement without resolving the underlying legal ambiguity about who is an employee. On balance, the benefits to misclassified workers outweigh the compliance burden, though the paperwork requirements are broad.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, and neither committee ever held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the Employee Misclassification Prevention Act on May 21, 2008, with 24 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Education and Labor and the Committee on Ways and Means on the day it was introduced [S1] [S5].
On June 2, 2008, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Income Security and Family Support, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S1] [S5].
No committee report, floor vote, or Senate action is listed; the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that save money by treating employees as independent contractors, and that would have faced doubled damages, new penalties, audits, and information sharing with the IRS, are better off because the bill never moved.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the provisions within its jurisdiction, including the unemployment tax and IRS referral sections.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored and the bill never advanced to a vote.

industries.industry: Employers that rely on independent contractors and misclassification
industries.note: These employers save on minimum wage, overtime, payroll taxes, and benefits by classifying workers as contractors. The bill would have imposed record-keeping, notice, doubled damages, fines, and targeted audits, and routed findings to the IRS.
Staffing firms that classify workers correctly would face only paperwork costs, but firms whose business model depends on contractor status would lose the wage and tax advantage.

States would have to build audit programs and administrative penalties as a condition of federal grants, adding administrative burden while recovering unemployment taxes currently lost to misclassification.
